newsitem.title: USA: Silver offtake in photography to increase - study.
newsitem.headline: Silver offtake in photography to increase - study.

text.p: Silver's use in photography is set to grow steadily over the next few years in the absence of any major rival picture-taking method in most sectors for the time being, a survey for producer-backed Silver Institute said.

Photography, which represents about a third of annual global silver demand, will consume 234 million ounces in the year 2000, up 7.3 percent from the 218 million ounces consumed in 1995, the survey conducted by photographic expert Peter Krause, vice president of consultancy Imaging/Technology Markets forecast.

"A lot of people are trying to come up with other photographic systems," Krause said. "So far none has had the quality of image, competitive price and convenience. Until such a system comes along that is better in these three respects, silver will continue to dominate in the amateur and X-Ray sectors."

The introduction of the so-called Advanced Photo System (APS) camera last year will rejeuvenate camera sales in the amateur sector, helping to boost silver demand from film sales even though the APS film is narrower and contains less metal, Krause said.
X-rays still remain the largest user of silver in photography, and consumption will rise from 86 million ounces in 1995 to 92 million ounces in 2000, Krause noted.
An ageing population in developed countries will call for more X-rays, Krause said.

However, a slight decline in the use of silver in professional photography was expected, with combined silver consumption from film and print usage shrinking from 38.5 million ounces in 1995 to 37 million in 2000.
The decline will be due to image setters using technology which skips film.
APS cameras already accounted for 15 percent of sales in Japan where most makers of the camera are based.
In the U.S. Krause expected APS cameras to account for 20 percent of amateur camera sales by the end of 1997.
The global use of silver in camera film is set to grow from 65 million ounces in 1995 to 75 million in 2000.
Digital imaging was too costly and dogged by poor image quality, and will only make its mark in professional market niches for the forseeable future, Krause said.

But the construction of multi-screen movie theaters in the U.S. and Europe has boosted the need for motion picture prints, increasing demand for silver in this sector from 10 million ounces in 1995 to 13 million ounces in 2000, Krause forecast.
